title: Burden of proof shifting under special statutes vs general criminal law
p1: Most people think one rule applies to every criminal case: the prosecution must always prove everything. But some special laws can change that balance in surprising ways.
p2: A common misconception is that the burden of proof can never shift. Under general criminal law, the prosecution usually carries the full burden to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. However, certain special statutes may place a limited burden on the accused after the prosecution first establishes specific facts.
p3: This does not mean a person must prove innocence from the beginning. It means the law may require the accused to explain or establish certain exceptions, defenses, or circumstances. The key difference is that the initial responsibility still starts with the prosecution. Knowing this distinction helps avoid a major misunderstanding about how criminal trials work.
conclusion: Do you think special statutes should allow a shift in the burden of proof, or should the same rule apply in every criminal case?
